cross_references.short_title: 18 U.S.C. §2511 — Federal Wiretap Act / ECPA Title I
cross_references.description: ECPA Title I (Wiretap Act) covers communication content in transit — the highest-protection tier with $10,000/violation civil damages. Pen Register Act (Title III) covers routing metadata — lowest-protection tier with no civil damages. The boundary between them (particularly the URL content question) directly affects damages calculation: if SIM swap account access URL logs = content, §2511 damages apply; if routing, no civil remedy for that metadata.

cross_references.short_title: 18 U.S.C. §§2701-2712 — Stored Communications Act / ECPA Title II
cross_references.description: ECPA Title II (SCA) covers stored communication content — $1,000/violation civil damages. Pen Register Act (Title III) covers routing metadata — no civil damages. The three titles together form a comprehensive electronic surveillance framework. Call routing records obtained under Pen Register Act procedures document the SIM swap's timeline and scale, supporting the SCA and Wiretap Act damages calculation.

cross_references.short_title: 47 C.F.R. §64.2010 — FCC CPNI Rules (AT&T Carrier Liability)
cross_references.description: AT&T's CPNI records (call routing logs, SIM swap processing records) are the primary evidence documenting the SIM swap attack. CPNI rules define what AT&T must protect; subpoenas to AT&T for those records in civil litigation use CPNI data types. The Pen Register Act framework explains why AT&T has this data and what it covers.

cross_references.short_title: 18 U.S.C. §1030 — Computer Fraud and Abuse Act
cross_references.description: Pen Register Act covers call routing metadata; CFAA covers the computer systems accessed using the intercepted credentials. URL access logs (which may be content or routing information) document CFAA unauthorized access events. The routing records establish when the SIM swap was active; CFAA covers what computer systems were accessed during that period.
